stem: A 51-year-old woman has had no menstrual bleeding for 9 months and has frequent night sweats. Which statement best describes her reproductive stage?

choices.text: She is postmenopausal because she has had more than 6 months of amenorrhea with vasomotor symptoms.
Her stage should be determined by a serum FSH level above 40 IU/L.
She is in the late menopause transition; menopause can be confirmed only after 12 months of amenorrhea.

rationale: Menopause is defined retrospectively by the final menstrual period after 12 months of amenorrhea. Amenorrhea of ≥60 days places her in the late transition (STRAW+10).

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Six months does not meet the 12-month criterion.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: STRAW+10 is anchored on bleeding pattern; FSH is supportive only and fluctuates.

learningObjective: Apply STRAW+10 menstrual criteria to stage the menopause transition.
author: AI draft

stem: Fezolinetant reduces vasomotor symptoms primarily by acting on which pathway?

choices.text: Blocking neurokinin B signaling at NK3 receptors on hypothalamic KNDy neurons
Inhibiting serotonin reuptake in the thermoregulatory center
Agonizing estrogen receptor-β in peripheral vasculature

rationale: Estrogen withdrawal leads to KNDy neuron hyperactivity and excess neurokinin B signaling to the thermoregulatory center. Fezolinetant is a selective NK3 receptor antagonist.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Describes SSRIs/SNRIs.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: VMS originate centrally; fezolinetant is not an estrogen receptor ligand.

learningObjective: Describe the KNDy mechanism underlying VMS and its pharmacologic target.
author: AI draft

stem: A 36-year-old woman has had 5 months of amenorrhea and hot flashes. Pregnancy test is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Reassure her that early perimenopause is common and recheck in a year
Measure FSH and estradiol (repeated), with TSH and prolactin, to evaluate for primary ovarian insufficiency
Begin a salivary hormone panel to guide compounded therapy

rationale: Amenorrhea before 40 warrants evaluation for POI; laboratory testing is appropriate in this age group, unlike typical perimenopause after 45.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Menopause before 40 is not normal and needs evaluation.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Salivary testing is unreliable and compounded therapy is not recommended.

learningObjective: Recognize when laboratory evaluation is indicated in suspected POI.
author: AI draft

stem: Which statement about androgens in midlife women is correct?

choices.text: A total testosterone below the reference range confirms female androgen insufficiency.
Adrenal androgens decline abruptly at the final menstrual period.
No serum androgen concentration defines female androgen insufficiency, so levels should not guide diagnosis.

rationale: No serum androgen level defines female androgen insufficiency; checking levels to diagnose or guide treatment of low desire is not recommended.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: There is no validated threshold.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Adrenal androgens rise moderately in the late transition and return toward baseline 1–2 years after the FMP.

learningObjective: Interpret the role of androgen testing in midlife women.
author: AI draft

stem: A 42-year-old woman undergoes bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for benign disease and declines estrogen. Compared with natural menopause, she is at increased risk of which long-term outcome?

choices.text: Dementia and cardiovascular disease
Ovarian cancer recurrence
Endometrial hyperplasia

rationale: Bilateral oophorectomy at or before 45 is associated with increased dementia and cardiovascular risk; estrogen until the average age of menopause appears to mitigate these risks.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Not relevant after benign oophorectomy.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Hyperplasia relates to unopposed estrogen, not estrogen deficiency.

learningObjective: Identify health risks of early surgical menopause.
author: AI draft

stem: A 63-year-old woman using low-dose vaginal estradiol for 2 years reports one episode of light spotting. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Reassure her that spotting is expected with vaginal estrogen
Evaluate with transvaginal ultrasound and/or endometrial sampling
Add oral micronized progesterone and reassess in 6 months

rationale: Any postmenopausal bleeding warrants evaluation, regardless of vaginal estrogen use.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Bleeding should not be attributed to therapy without evaluation.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Progestogen is not indicated with low-dose vaginal ET and does not replace evaluation.

learningObjective: Manage postmenopausal bleeding in women using vaginal estrogen.
author: AI draft

stem: A 47-year-old woman who smokes a pack per day requests contraception and has heavy irregular bleeding. Which option is most appropriate?

choices.text: Low-dose combined oral contraceptive
Contraceptive vaginal ring
Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system

rationale: Estrogen-containing contraception is inappropriate in a smoker over 35. The LNG-IUS provides contraception and treats heavy bleeding.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Contraindicated in smokers over 35.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Also estrogen-containing.

learningObjective: Select contraception in perimenopausal women with estrogen contraindications.
author: AI draft

stem: In which situation is serum FSH measurement most useful to assess menopausal status?

choices.text: A 49-year-old with a levonorgestrel IUD and new vasomotor symptoms
A 50-year-old with irregular cycles and hot flashes
A 55-year-old with 2 years of amenorrhea

rationale: Testing may help when bleeding cannot be used to assess status, such as with an LNG-IUD or after hysterectomy.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Clinical picture is sufficient; FSH fluctuates.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: She is clearly postmenopausal.

learningObjective: Identify appropriate indications for hormone testing.
author: AI draft

stem: Approximately what proportion of women with endometrial cancer present with abnormal uterine bleeding?

choices.text: About 50%
About 70%
About 90%

rationale: About 90% of women diagnosed with uterine cancer present with abnormal bleeding — the basis for evaluating all postmenopausal bleeding.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Underestimates.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Underestimates.

learningObjective: Recall the presentation of endometrial cancer.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman on continuous combined estrogen–progestogen therapy started 3 months ago reports irregular light bleeding. She has no other symptoms. What is the most appropriate approach?

choices.text: Immediate endometrial biopsy
Stop HT permanently
Counsel that unscheduled bleeding is common early; evaluate if it persists beyond about 6 months or is heavy

rationale: Unscheduled bleeding is common in the first months of continuous combined therapy; persistent bleeding beyond ~6 months warrants evaluation.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not required this early for light bleeding without risk factors.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Not indicated.

learningObjective: Manage expected bleeding patterns on EPT.
author: AI draft

stem: What proportion of women experience vasomotor symptoms for more than 10 years?

choices.text: About one-third
About 5%
About two-thirds

rationale: VMS last a mean of 7–9 years, and roughly one-third of women experience them for more than 10 years.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Underestimates; ~10% have VMS >20 years.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Overestimates.

learningObjective: Counsel on expected VMS duration.
author: AI draft

stem: In nonhormone VMS trials, which patient characteristic is associated with a greater placebo response?

choices.text: Higher BMI
Greater anxiety
Surgical menopause

rationale: Women with more anxiety show a higher placebo response; placebo improvement rates range from 20% to 66%.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not identified as the predictor.

author: AI draft

stem: A healthy 52-year-old, 1 year past her final period, has 10 moderate-to-severe hot flashes daily and no contraindications. What is the most effective treatment?

choices.text: Paced respiration training
Black cohosh extract
Systemic hormone therapy

rationale: HT is the most effective treatment for VMS and has a favorable benefit–risk ratio in women <60 or within 10 years of menopause.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not recommended (Level I).
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Supplements not recommended; no benefit over placebo.

stem: Which comorbidity is a recognized risk factor for more bothersome vasomotor symptoms?

choices.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
Hypothyroidism treated to euthyroid state
Iron deficiency

rationale: Comorbidities associated with VMS include thyroid disease, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea and chronic pain conditions.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Thyroid disease is a risk factor, but the euthyroid treated state is not the listed association.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not listed.

learningObjective: Identify risk factors for VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman asks whether regular exercise will reduce her hot flashes. Based on the 2023 nonhormone statement, how should you counsel her?

choices.text: Exercise is Level I recommended for VMS reduction.
Exercise is not recommended specifically for VMS, though it has broad health benefits.
Exercise worsens VMS and should be avoided.

rationale: Exercise, yoga and cooling techniques are Level II not recommended for VMS treatment; exercise remains beneficial for overall health.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Evidence was insufficient for recommendation.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not supported.

learningObjective: Counsel accurately about lifestyle measures for VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: A 54-year-old with an intact uterus starts transdermal estradiol for VMS. Which addition is required?

choices.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen
Annual endometrial biopsy without a progestogen
A progestogen (or LNG-IUS), unless using CEE with bazedoxifene

rationale: Systemic estrogen with an intact uterus requires endometrial protection with a progestogen, LNG-IUS (off-label), or a TSEC.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Does not protect the endometrium.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Surveillance does not replace protection.

learningObjective: Ensure endometrial protection with systemic estrogen.
author: AI draft

stem: A 66-year-old woman has used estradiol and micronized progesterone since age 52 for VMS, which recur when she tries to stop. She is otherwise healthy. What is the most appropriate counseling?

choices.text: Continuation can be reasonable with shared decision-making and periodic reevaluation of benefits and risks.
She must discontinue HT because she is over 65.
Switch to compounded estriol to lower risk.

rationale: There are no data to support routine discontinuation at 65; longer use for documented indications such as persistent VMS can be appropriate with periodic reassessment.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: No mandatory stop age.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Compounded products are not recommended and not shown safer.

learningObjective: Counsel on HT duration beyond 65.
author: AI draft

stem: In the WHI estrogen-alone (CEE) arm, what was observed for breast cancer?

choices.text: Increased incidence with HR about 1.3
Reduced incidence and reduced breast cancer mortality
No effect on incidence or mortality

rationale: CEE alone was associated with reduced breast cancer incidence that persisted at long-term follow-up, and reduced breast cancer mortality.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Describes CEE + MPA.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: A reduction was observed.

learningObjective: Distinguish breast cancer outcomes for ET vs EPT in WHI.
author: AI draft

stem: A 50-year-old with a BMI of 36 and migraine without aura has bothersome VMS. Which estrogen route is preferred?

choices.text: Oral conjugated estrogens
Compounded estradiol pellet
Transdermal estradiol

rationale: Transdermal estradiol avoids first-pass hepatic effects and is associated with lower VTE and stroke risk in observational data; stable levels may also help migraine.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Oral route increases VTE risk relative to transdermal.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Pellets are not recommended.

author: AI draft

stem: Under the FDA class labeling changes for menopausal hormone therapy announced in 2025 and approved beginning February 2026, which boxed warning was retained?

choices.text: Endometrial cancer for systemic estrogen-alone products
Probable dementia for all systemic products
Breast cancer for all estrogen-containing products

rationale: Statements on cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and probable dementia were removed from the boxed warning; the endometrial cancer boxed warning was retained for systemic estrogen-alone products.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Removed throughout labeling.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Removed from the boxed warning; retained elsewhere in labeling.

author: AI draft

stem: In WHI participants aged 50–59 at enrollment, what was the effect of hormone therapy on all-cause mortality?

choices.text: Significantly increased
Significantly reduced
Not assessed

rationale: In women aged 50–59, all-cause mortality was significantly reduced (HR ~0.69), supporting the favorable profile of early initiation.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Incorrect direction.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: It was assessed in age-stratified analyses.

stem: A 48-year-old on tamoxifen for ER-positive breast cancer has severe hot flashes. Which agent is most appropriate?

choices.text: Paroxetine 20 mg daily
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily
Venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily, titrating as needed

rationale: Paroxetine and fluoxetine strongly inhibit CYP2D6, reducing conversion of tamoxifen to endoxifen. Venlafaxine has minimal CYP2D6 effect.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitor and not recommended for VMS.

learningObjective: Choose a nonhormone agent compatible with tamoxifen.
author: AI draft

stem: Which intervention is Level I NOT recommended for vasomotor symptoms in the 2023 nonhormone position statement?

choices.text: Paced respiration
Clinical hypnosis
Cognitive-behavioral therapy

rationale: Paced respiration is not recommended (Level I). CBT and hypnosis are recommended (Level I).

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Recommended, Level I.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Recommended, Level I.

learningObjective: Distinguish recommended from not-recommended mind–body interventions.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman starting fezolinetant asks about monitoring. Per the 2024 boxed warning, what is required?

choices.text: No laboratory monitoring is needed
Hepatic tests at baseline, monthly for the first 3 months, then at 6 and 9 months
Annual lipid panel and mammogram

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Monitoring is required.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not the labeled monitoring requirement.

stem: A 55-year-old with prior DVT has frequent night sweats that disrupt sleep. She prefers a medication taken once at night. Which is most appropriate?

choices.text: Clonidine 0.1 mg at bedtime
Pregabalin 150 mg twice daily
Gabapentin at bedtime, titrated toward 900 mg/day or higher as tolerated

rationale: Gabapentin (Level I) reduces VMS; bedtime dosing leverages sedation for VMS-related sleep disruption. Systemic HT is avoided after VTE.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not recommended; less effective with more adverse effects.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Not recommended (Level III; Schedule V).

learningObjective: Select nonhormone therapy for nocturnal VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: Which SSRI is FDA approved specifically for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms?

choices.text: Paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg daily
Escitalopram 10 mg daily
Sertraline 50 mg daily

rationale: Low-dose paroxetine salt 7.5 mg was the first nonhormone FDA-approved therapy for VMS.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Effective but off-label for VMS.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not recommended for VMS.

learningObjective: Recall FDA-approved nonhormone VMS agents.
author: AI draft

stem: A 74-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment has bothersome VMS. Which nonhormone agent should be avoided?

choices.text: Escitalopram
Oxybutynin
Cognitive-behavioral therapy

rationale: Oxybutynin is anticholinergic; long-term use may be associated with cognitive decline, particularly in older adults.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Reasonable option.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: No cognitive risk.

learningObjective: Recognize anticholinergic risk with oxybutynin.
author: AI draft

stem: A 60-year-old with an intact uterus starts the estradiol 2 mg vaginal ring (releasing ~7.5 µg/day) for GSM. Which is correct?

choices.text: A progestogen is required for endometrial protection.
This ring will also adequately treat her moderate VMS.
No progestogen is needed and routine endometrial surveillance is not recommended.

rationale: The low-dose estradiol ring is local therapy; no progestogen is indicated and asymptomatic surveillance is not recommended.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Applies to the systemic-dose estradiol acetate ring.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Low-dose local therapy does not treat VMS.

learningObjective: Differentiate local from systemic vaginal rings.
author: AI draft

stem: What is first-line therapy for mild genitourinary syndrome of menopause?

choices.text: Regular vaginal moisturizers plus lubricants with sexual activity
Fractional CO2 laser
Systemic estradiol

rationale: Nonhormone lubricants and long-acting moisturizers are first-line (Level A).

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Insufficient evidence; not recommended routinely.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Local therapy is preferred for isolated GSM.

learningObjective: Apply the GSM treatment ladder.
author: AI draft

stem: Which finding is typical of GSM on office testing?

choices.text: Vaginal pH below 4.5 with abundant lactobacilli
Vaginal pH greater than 5.0 with parabasal cells
Clue cells with positive whiff test

rationale: Hypoestrogenism raises vaginal pH (>5.0) and increases parabasal cells with reduced lactobacilli; these tests support but are not required for diagnosis.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Describes the estrogenized premenopausal vagina.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Suggests bacterial vaginosis.

learningObjective: Recognize objective findings in GSM.
author: AI draft

stem: A 58-year-old with moderate dyspareunia due to GSM declines all vaginal products. Which prescription option fits her preference?

choices.text: Prasterone 6.5 mg vaginal insert
Vaginal estradiol tablet
Ospemifene 60 mg orally daily

rationale: Ospemifene is the only oral prescription option for moderate–severe dyspareunia due to menopause.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Vaginal product.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Vaginal product.

learningObjective: Select GSM therapy by route preference.
author: AI draft

stem: A 66-year-old has had three culture-proven UTIs in the past year and signs of vaginal atrophy. Which intervention has evidence to reduce recurrence?

choices.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen
Systemic oral estradiol
Vaginal CO2 laser

rationale: Low-dose vaginal estrogen may prevent recurrent UTIs in postmenopausal women. Systemic HT has no urinary indication.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Not indicated for urinary outcomes.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Insufficient evidence.

author: AI draft

stem: Systemic hormone therapy has what effect on stress urinary incontinence?

choices.text: It improves stress incontinence and is FDA approved for it.
It may worsen stress urinary incontinence.
It has no relationship to urinary symptoms.

rationale: Systemic HT does not improve urinary incontinence and may increase stress urinary incontinence.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: HT has no FDA urinary indication.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: An adverse association has been observed.

learningObjective: Recall urinary effects of systemic HT.
author: AI draft

stem: A 53-year-old with chronic insomnia but no VMS asks for a sleep treatment. What is first-line?

choices.text: Systemic estradiol
Long-term zolpidem
Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)

rationale: CBT-I is first-line for insomnia in menopausal women with durable benefit. No HT is FDA approved for insomnia.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not indicated for insomnia without VMS.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Not first-line.

stem: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman has distressing low sexual desire. Her total testosterone is low-normal. How should HSDD be diagnosed?

choices.text: Clinically, based on history and distress, after addressing contributing factors
By total testosterone below the female reference range
By free androgen index

wrongAnswerRationales.b: No threshold defines androgen insufficiency.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Also not diagnostic.

author: AI draft

stem: Which statement about hormone therapy and cognition is correct?

choices.text: HT is recommended to prevent dementia if started within 10 years of menopause.
HT is not recommended at any age to prevent or treat cognitive decline or dementia.
HT reduces dementia when initiated after age 65.

rationale: HT is not recommended for cognitive indications at any age; initiation ≥65 increased dementia in WHIMS.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: WHIMS showed increased risk.

stem: A perimenopausal woman with a history of major depression has 3 weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia and poor sleep. What is first-line management?

Watchful waiting until menopause
Antidepressant therapy and/or psychotherapy

Increase the oral estrogen dose
Add oral DHEA supplements

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Would further increase SHBG.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Oral DHEA supplements are not recommended.

author: AI draft

stem: A 58-year-old with a prior unprovoked PE has bothersome VMS. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

A nonhormone therapy such as an SSRI/SNRI, gabapentin or an NK antagonist
CEE with bazedoxifene

author: AI draft

stem: Which is an FDA-approved indication for systemic hormone therapy?

Prevention of type 2 diabetes
Prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Observed effect only.

stem: A 52-year-old whose mother and sister had VTE wants systemic HT. She has never had a clot. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Consider thrombophilia evaluation and favor transdermal therapy if HT is chosen
Start oral estrogen without further evaluation
Systemic HT is absolutely contraindicated

HT is not indicated for cardioprotection, and initiation this far from menopause carries higher absolute CV risk.
HT is appropriate if delivered transdermally.

author: AI draft

Only weight loss to normal BMI
3% to 10% of body weight

stem: A 70-year-old has received denosumab for 4 years and wants to stop. What is the most appropriate plan?

Stop denosumab and recheck DXA in 2 years
Take a 1-year drug holiday, then restart

stem: A 67-year-old has taken alendronate for 5 years. She has never fractured and her hip T-score is now −1.9. What is reasonable?

Continue indefinitely without reassessment

Normal bone density
Osteoporosis — the diagnosis persists

At least 2,000 mg from supplements
About 600 mg

At birth, before any atresia

Use a lower dose adjusted for renal function

rationale: Gabapentin is renally excreted, so dosing must be reduced in CKD. Bedtime dosing suits night sweats and limits dizziness and somnolence.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Gabapentin is cleared unchanged by the kidneys.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: It can be used with renal dose adjustment.

learningObjective: Adjust gabapentin dosing for renal function.

stem: A woman who has taken venlafaxine 75 mg daily for hot flashes for a year wants to stop. What is the best advice?

choices.text: Taper the dose over a few weeks to avoid discontinuation symptoms
Stop abruptly; discontinuation symptoms occur only at antidepressant doses
Switch to paroxetine first, then stop

rationale: SNRIs and SSRIs, especially short half-life agents like venlafaxine and paroxetine, can cause dizziness, irritability and flu-like symptoms if stopped abruptly.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Discontinuation symptoms can occur at VMS doses, especially with venlafaxine.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: An unnecessary switch; paroxetine also causes discontinuation symptoms.

learningObjective: Safely discontinue SSRI/SNRI therapy.
author: AI draft

stem: How does cognitive-behavioral therapy mainly help menopausal vasomotor symptoms?

choices.text: It mainly reduces hot flash bother and interference
It eliminates hot flashes in most women within 2 weeks
It is recommended only for breast cancer survivors

rationale: CBT (MENOS 1 and 2) improves VMS bother, interference, sleep and quality of life. Clinical hypnosis reduces both frequency and severity.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: CBT reduces bother but does not abolish VMS.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: MENOS trials showed benefit in women with and without breast cancer.

author: AI draft

stem: Which mind–body therapy has randomized trial evidence for reducing hot flash frequency and severity?

choices.text: Mindfulness-based stress reduction
Paced respiration
Clinical hypnosis

rationale: Clinical hypnosis is recommended (Level I) and has reduced VMS frequency by roughly 50–70% in trials.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Evidence is insufficient, so it is not recommended for VMS.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Trials showed no benefit; it is not recommended.

learningObjective: Identify effective mind–body interventions for VMS.
author: AI draft

stem: A 54-year-old with poorly controlled hypertension wants nonhormone treatment for hot flashes. Which agent needs the most caution?

choices.text: Gabapentin
Venlafaxine
Cognitive-behavioral therapy

rationale: Venlafaxine can raise blood pressure in a dose-related way. Monitor blood pressure, or choose another option when hypertension is uncontrolled.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Gabapentin does not raise blood pressure.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: CBT has no cardiovascular effects.

learningObjective: Match nonhormone agents to comorbidities.
author: AI draft

stem: A woman starting elinzanetant asks about the timing of her dose. What is the best counseling?

choices.text: In the morning on an empty stomach, to avoid insomnia
Once daily at bedtime, because it can cause somnolence
Only as needed, at the onset of each hot flash episode

rationale: Somnolence/fatigue and headache are among the most common adverse effects of elinzanetant, so bedtime dosing is recommended. Patients should be cautious with driving if drowsy.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: The concern is sedation, not insomnia.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: It is a scheduled daily medication.

learningObjective: Counsel on elinzanetant administration and adverse effects.
author: AI draft

stem: A 57-year-old with a prior DVT has bothersome hot flashes and a new major depressive episode. Which option best addresses both?

choices.text: An SNRI such as venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine
Low-dose transdermal estradiol with progesterone
Gabapentin titrated to 900 mg at bedtime

rationale: SSRIs/SNRIs are recommended for VMS and are first-line for depression, so one agent can treat both in a woman who should avoid systemic HT.

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Gabapentin treats VMS but not depression.

stem: How does the natural history of GSM differ from that of vasomotor symptoms?

choices.text: It usually resolves within 5 years of the final period
It affects only women who are sexually active
It is chronic and progressive without treatment

wrongAnswerRationales.b: GSM affects vulvovaginal and urinary tissues regardless of sexual activity.

stem: Which describes intravaginal prasterone (DHEA)?

choices.text: A daily oral SERM tablet with estrogenic vaginal effects
A systemic androgen that requires progestogen co-therapy
A nightly 6.5-mg vaginal insert converted locally

rationale: Prasterone is FDA approved for moderate to severe dyspareunia due to menopause. Its main adverse effect is vaginal discharge.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: That describes ospemifene.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Serum levels remain in the postmenopausal range and no progestogen is required.

learningObjective: Recall the formulation and mechanism of vaginal DHEA.
author: AI draft

stem: A 57-year-old is starting ospemifene for dyspareunia. Which counseling point is most important?

choices.text: It must be combined with a progestogen to protect the endometrium
It can worsen hot flashes and carries a stroke and VTE warning
It is preferred for women with a history of breast cancer

rationale: Ospemifene is an oral SERM that is estrogenic on vaginal epithelium. Hot flashes are its most common adverse effect, and it shares the SERM thromboembolic warning; stop it before prolonged immobilization.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Ospemifene does not require a progestogen.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: In the US it is not approved for women with breast cancer.

learningObjective: Counsel on ospemifene adverse effects.
author: AI draft

stem: A 56-year-old has used transdermal estradiol with progesterone for 2 years. Her hot flashes have resolved, but vaginal dryness and dyspareunia persist. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Add low-dose vaginal estrogen
Increase the systemic estrogen dose
Tell her that systemic HT always treats GSM, so another diagnosis is likely

rationale: A substantial minority of women on systemic HT still have GSM symptoms. Adding local vaginal estrogen is often effective.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Raising systemic exposure is unnecessary; local therapy targets the tissue.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Persistent GSM on systemic HT is common.

learningObjective: Manage GSM that persists on systemic hormone therapy.
author: AI draft

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes vaginal moisturizers from lubricants?

choices.text: Moisturizers are used on a schedule; lubricants are used with sex
Lubricants restore vaginal epithelium when used several times a week
Moisturizers should be applied only right before intercourse

rationale: Both are first-line for mild GSM. Choosing products with appropriate osmolality and pH and avoiding irritants such as fragrances helps limit irritation.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Lubricants reduce friction but do not change the tissue.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Moisturizers are used on a schedule, for example 2–3 times weekly.

learningObjective: Differentiate moisturizers from lubricants.
author: AI draft

stem: After 4 months of vaginal estrogen, a 60-year-old's vaginal epithelium looks healthy, but she still has pain at the introitus with penetration and tender, tight levator muscles. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Double the dose and frequency of vaginal estrogen
Refer for a series of fractional CO₂ laser treatments
Pelvic floor physical therapy with vaginal dilators

rationale: Severe or longstanding GSM can lead to pelvic floor hypertonus, which needs pelvic floor physical therapy and dilators along with treatment of the epithelium.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: The epithelium has responded; the remaining problem is muscular.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Laser is not FDA approved for GSM and does not address pelvic floor hypertonus.

learningObjective: Recognize and treat pelvic floor dysfunction coexisting with GSM.
author: AI draft

stem: What is the status of fractional CO₂ and erbium lasers for GSM?

choices.text: They are FDA approved as first-line therapy for GSM
They are not FDA approved, and long-term data are insufficient
They are preferred over vaginal estrogen for breast cancer survivors

rationale: In 2018 the FDA warned about burns, scarring and chronic pain after vaginal energy-based procedures. The 2020 GSM statement does not recommend them outside trials.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: No energy-based device is approved for GSM.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Evidence is insufficient to recommend them over established options.

learningObjective: Recall the regulatory and evidence status of vaginal laser therapy.
author: AI draft

stem: A 62-year-old has urinary urgency, frequency and signs of vaginal atrophy on exam. Urinalysis is negative. Which hormonal option is most likely to improve her urgency?

choices.text: Oral conjugated estrogens
Low-dose vaginal estrogen
No hormonal option, because estrogen has no effect on bladder symptoms

rationale: Vaginal estrogen improves urgency, frequency and overactive bladder symptoms, can augment antimuscarinic therapy, and reduces recurrent UTIs.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Systemic HT can worsen urinary incontinence.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Vaginal estrogen improves overactive bladder symptoms.

learningObjective: Use vaginal estrogen for urinary symptoms of GSM.
author: AI draft

stem: A 63-year-old has intense vulvar itching. Exam shows white, crinkled plaques around the vulva and perianal area, with labial resorption. What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: High-potency topical corticosteroid for lichen sclerosus
Low-dose vaginal estrogen alone for GSM
Oral fluconazole for vulvovaginal candidiasis

rationale: Lichen sclerosus is in the differential of GSM. It causes pruritus, white plaques in a figure-of-eight pattern and architectural loss, and it needs long-term surveillance because of the risk of vulvar cancer.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Perianal involvement and architectural change suggest lichen sclerosus, not GSM.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: The findings are not those of candidiasis.

learningObjective: Differentiate lichen sclerosus from GSM.
author: AI draft

stem: A 64-year-old uses a 10-µg vaginal estradiol insert twice weekly and has no bleeding. She asks if she needs yearly endometrial ultrasound. What is the best response?

choices.text: Yes, annual ultrasound is required with any vaginal estrogen
She needs a cyclic progestogen to protect the endometrium
No routine surveillance; report any vaginal bleeding

rationale: Systemic absorption from low-dose vaginal estrogen is minimal and does not raise endometrial cancer risk. Postmenopausal bleeding still requires evaluation.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Low-dose vaginal estrogen does not require surveillance.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: No progestogen is needed with low-dose vaginal estrogen.

learningObjective: Apply surveillance rules for low-dose vaginal estrogen.
author: AI draft

stem: A 56-year-old reports daytime sleepiness and her partner notes loud snoring. She has hypertension and a BMI of 33. Her hot flashes are mild. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Start hormone therapy to consolidate her sleep
Prescribe a sedative-hypnotic at bedtime
Evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea

rationale: OSA becomes more common after menopause and is linked to hypertension and cardiometabolic risk. Snoring with daytime sleepiness should prompt testing.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Her symptoms suggest a primary sleep disorder rather than VMS-related awakenings.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Sedatives can worsen untreated sleep apnea.

learningObjective: Recognize obstructive sleep apnea in midlife women.
examTrapTags: attributing all sleep problems to menopause
author: AI draft

stem: Which factor most strongly predicts a major depressive episode during the menopause transition?

choices.text: Earlier age at menarche
A prior history of major depression
Use of oral contraceptives in her 20s

rationale: Women with a history of MDD have a markedly higher risk of recurrence in perimenopause. VMS, sleep disruption and stressful life events also contribute.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not a strong predictor.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not associated with perimenopausal depression.

learningObjective: Identify risk factors for perimenopausal depression.
author: AI draft

stem: Which statement about estrogen and mood is best supported?

choices.text: It may help perimenopausal depression but is not FDA approved for it
It is effective for depression in late postmenopausal women
It prevents the onset of depression in women who are not depressed

rationale: Some evidence suggests antidepressant effects of estrogen in perimenopause, particularly with VMS. Evidence is limited, and established treatments are first-line for major depression.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Trials in older postmenopausal women have not shown benefit.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Trials in nondepressed women have not shown mood benefit.

learningObjective: Interpret evidence on estrogen and mood.
author: AI draft

stem: A 49-year-old in the menopause transition worries about trouble finding words and forgetfulness. Her exam and screening cognitive test are normal. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Reassure her that these changes are common and usually transient
Start hormone therapy to lower her future dementia risk
Order amyloid PET imaging to exclude early Alzheimer disease

rationale: SWAN found subtle, temporary declines in processing speed and verbal memory during the transition that rebound after menopause. Dementia before age 64 is rare.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: HT is not recommended to prevent or treat cognitive decline.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not indicated for subjective complaints with a normal evaluation.

learningObjective: Counsel about transition-related cognitive complaints.
author: AI draft

stem: What did the WHI Memory Study (WHIMS) find in women aged 65 and older?

choices.text: Estrogen alone markedly reduced dementia risk
Hormone therapy improved global cognitive scores
Estrogen plus MPA increased probable dementia

rationale: WHIMS, which started HT at 65 or older, found more probable dementia with CEE+MPA. Findings may not apply to younger women starting near menopause. HT is not recommended to prevent dementia at any age.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: No protective effect was found.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: No cognitive benefit was seen.

learningObjective: Recall WHIMS findings and their limits.
author: AI draft

stem: Which is a modifiable risk factor for dementia that midlife women should be counseled about?

choices.text: Early menarche
Physical inactivity
Use of low-dose vaginal estrogen

rationale: Modifiable risk factors include physical inactivity, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, smoking, excessive alcohol, low social contact, hearing loss and traumatic brain injury.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Not modifiable and not a recognized dementia risk factor.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not associated with dementia risk.

learningObjective: Counsel on modifiable dementia risk factors.
author: AI draft

stem: A 57-year-old with HSDD starts transdermal testosterone at about one-tenth of the male dose. How should she be monitored?

choices.text: Titrate the dose to the upper male reference range
Check levels at baseline and 3–6 weeks; stop if no benefit by 6 months
No monitoring is needed because adverse effects do not occur in women

rationale: The Global Consensus Position Statement recommends baseline and follow-up total testosterone to keep levels in the premenopausal range, with a therapeutic trial of up to 6 months.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: The goal is the premenopausal female range.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Levels are monitored to avoid androgen excess.

learningObjective: Monitor testosterone therapy for HSDD.
author: AI draft

stem: What is the status of testosterone products for postmenopausal women in the United States?

choices.text: None is FDA approved for women; male products are used off-label
Testosterone pellets are FDA approved for women with HSDD
Compounded creams are preferred because they are FDA regulated

rationale: Off-label transdermal testosterone in physiologic doses modestly improves desire, arousal, orgasm and satisfying events in postmenopausal women with HSDD. Long-term safety is not established.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Pellets are not approved for women and can cause supraphysiologic levels.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Compounded products are not FDA regulated for dose accuracy.

learningObjective: Recall the regulatory status and dosing of testosterone for women.
author: AI draft

stem: Flibanserin and bremelanotide are FDA approved for HSDD in which population?

choices.text: Postmenopausal women
Women of any age with GSM-related dyspareunia
Premenopausal women

rationale: Both are approved only for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD. For postmenopausal women, off-label testosterone is the main pharmacologic option.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Neither is approved for postmenopausal women.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: They treat low desire, not dyspareunia.

learningObjective: Recall approved indications for HSDD drugs.
author: AI draft

stem: Which is a core component of CBT for insomnia (CBT-I)?

choices.text: Scheduled daytime naps to make up lost sleep
Sleep hygiene education alone
Sleep restriction and stimulus control

rationale: CBT-I combines sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring and relaxation. It is first-line for insomnia in midlife women and has durable benefit.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Napping is discouraged because it reduces sleep drive.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Sleep hygiene alone is not effective as monotherapy.

learningObjective: Identify components of CBT-I.
author: AI draft

stem: A 52-year-old with systemic lupus erythematosus and positive antiphospholipid antibodies has bothersome hot flashes. What is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.text: Oral estradiol with a progestogen
Nonhormone therapy
Transdermal estradiol, which is safe in all women with lupus

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Antiphospholipid antibodies greatly increase thrombotic risk; systemic HT should be avoided.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: HT may be considered only in stable SLE without antiphospholipid antibodies.

learningObjective: Apply HT contraindications in autoimmune disease.
author: AI draft

stem: What effect does hormone therapy have on new-onset type 2 diabetes?

choices.text: It reduces the incidence by about 30%
It increases the incidence by about 30%
It has no effect on the incidence

rationale: Oral estrogen appears to have a greater effect on glucose metabolism than transdermal. HT should not be prescribed to prevent diabetes.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Trials show a reduction, not an increase.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: WHI and HERS both showed reduced incidence.

learningObjective: Recall the effect of HT on diabetes risk.
author: AI draft

stem: A 53-year-old with well-controlled hypertension on lisinopril has bothersome hot flashes. What is the most appropriate statement?

choices.text: It is not a contraindication; transdermal estradiol is reasonable
Hypertension is an absolute contraindication to any form of HT
Oral estrogen is preferred because it lowers blood pressure

rationale: Transdermal estrogen avoids hepatic stimulation of angiotensinogen and is generally preferred in women with hypertension or other cardiovascular risk factors.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Controlled hypertension is not a contraindication.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Oral estrogen can raise blood pressure slightly via renin substrate.

learningObjective: Prescribe HT safely in women with controlled hypertension.
author: AI draft

stem: A 56-year-old had a coronary stent placed 2 years ago and now has bothersome hot flashes. What is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.text: Transdermal estradiol for its secondary-prevention benefit
Oral HT to reduce recurrent coronary events, based on HERS
Nonhormone therapy, such as an SNRI or gabapentin

rationale: Women with established coronary disease should avoid systemic HT. HT is not recommended for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: HT does not prevent recurrent coronary events.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: HERS showed no benefit and an early increase in events.

learningObjective: Manage VMS in women with established ASCVD.

stem: A 51-year-old with no personal history of VTE is found to be heterozygous for factor V Leiden. She has severe hot flashes. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Oral conjugated estrogens, since she has never had a clot
Nonhormone therapy first; transdermal estradiol if HT is chosen
Avoid all estrogen, including low-dose vaginal products

wrongAnswerRationales.c: Low-dose vaginal estrogen has minimal absorption.

author: AI draft

stem: A 70-year-old with a prior ischemic stroke has dyspareunia from GSM that has not responded to moisturizers. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Systemic transdermal hormone therapy
Low-dose vaginal estrogen
Oral ospemifene 60 mg daily

rationale: Low-dose vaginal estrogen keeps serum estrogen in the postmenopausal range, so it may be considered in women with prior CVD, stroke or VTE.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Systemic HT is contraindicated after stroke.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: It carries warnings for stroke and VTE.

learningObjective: Use local therapy for GSM in women with cardiovascular contraindications.
author: AI draft

stem: What is the effect of hormone therapy on body weight?

choices.text: HT does not cause weight gain and may limit central fat gain
HT causes average weight gain of about 5 kg in the first year
HT is FDA approved for weight management after menopause

rationale: Midlife weight gain is driven mainly by aging and lifestyle. Fear of weight gain should not deter appropriate HT.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Trials do not show HT-related weight gain.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: HT has no weight indication.

learningObjective: Correct misconceptions about HT and weight.

stem: Which change in body composition is attributed to menopause itself rather than to chronological aging?

choices.text: Most of the total weight gained during midlife
An increase in lean muscle mass relative to fat
A shift toward central (visceral) fat distribution

rationale: Estrogen loss is associated with redistribution of fat to the abdomen, contributing to metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk even without weight gain.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Total weight gain reflects aging and lifestyle more than menopause.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Lean mass declines with age.

learningObjective: Distinguish menopause-related body composition change from aging.
author: AI draft

stem: Which lipid change occurs around the final menstrual period?

choices.text: LDL cholesterol falls as estradiol declines
Lipid changes are due only to aging, not menopause
LDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B rise

rationale: The menopause-related rise in LDL-C and apoB contributes to the rise in cardiovascular risk after menopause. Lipid screening every 1–2 years is reasonable from age 55 to 65.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: SWAN showed a menopause-specific rise in LDL around the FMP.

learningObjective: Recall menopause-related lipid changes.
author: AI draft

stem: A 55-year-old with hypothyroidism on a stable levothyroxine dose starts oral estradiol. What monitoring is appropriate?

choices.text: No monitoring, because estrogen does not affect thyroid replacement
Recheck TSH in 6–12 weeks, because oral estrogen raises TBG
Stop levothyroxine for as long as she takes estrogen

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Oral estrogen increases TBG and can raise levothyroxine requirements.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Thyroid replacement must continue.

author: AI draft

stem: A 66-year-old has a femoral neck T-score of −2.1 and no prior fracture. FRAX gives a 10-year hip fracture probability of 3.4% and a major osteoporotic fracture probability of 17%. What is recommended?

choices.text: Start pharmacologic therapy
No treatment until her T-score reaches −2.5
Calcium and vitamin D only

wrongAnswerRationales.b: High FRAX risk with osteopenia meets treatment thresholds.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: These do not prevent fracture alone in women meeting treatment thresholds.

learningObjective: Apply FRAX thresholds to treatment decisions.
author: AI draft

stem: A 68-year-old fractured her hip after tripping from standing height. Her DXA T-score is −1.8. What is her diagnosis?

choices.text: Osteoporosis, warranting pharmacologic therapy
Osteopenia; repeat DXA in 2 years
Normal bone; the fracture was traumatic

rationale: A hip or vertebral fragility fracture establishes clinical osteoporosis regardless of BMD and indicates high risk of further fracture.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: A low-trauma hip fracture establishes the diagnosis regardless of T-score.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: A fall from standing height is low-trauma.

learningObjective: Diagnose osteoporosis based on fragility fracture.
author: AI draft

stem: How should oral alendronate be taken?

choices.text: With breakfast, to reduce stomach upset
At bedtime, together with calcium supplements
Fasting, with water, staying upright for 30 minutes

rationale: Oral bisphosphonates are poorly absorbed. Correct dosing maximizes absorption and lowers the risk of esophagitis.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Food sharply reduces absorption.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Calcium blocks absorption, and lying down raises esophageal risk.

learningObjective: Counsel on oral bisphosphonate administration.
author: AI draft

stem: A 74-year-old with osteoporosis has a creatinine clearance of 28 mL/min. Which treatment is most appropriate?

choices.text: Annual intravenous zoledronic acid
Denosumab every 6 months
Weekly oral alendronate

rationale: Denosumab is not renally cleared, but hypocalcemia risk is higher in advanced CKD. It must not be stopped without follow-on therapy.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Contraindicated with creatinine clearance below 35 mL/min.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Not recommended with creatinine clearance below 35 mL/min.

author: AI draft

stem: For a woman at moderate fracture risk who has stable BMD on intravenous zoledronic acid, when may a drug holiday be considered?

choices.text: After 1 infusion
After 3 annual infusions
After 10 annual infusions

rationale: A holiday may be considered after about 5 years of oral or 3 years of IV bisphosphonate in moderate-risk women. High-risk women may continue up to 10 years oral or 6 years IV.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Too early to assess or bank benefit.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Holidays are considered much earlier for moderate-risk women.

learningObjective: Time bisphosphonate drug holidays.
author: AI draft

stem: A 70-year-old with very high fracture risk (multiple vertebral fractures) had a myocardial infarction 6 months ago. Which anabolic agent should be avoided?

choices.text: Romosozumab
Teriparatide
Abaloparatide

rationale: Romosozumab has a boxed warning for MI, stroke and cardiovascular death and should not be started within a year of MI or stroke. PTH/PTHrP analogs are alternatives.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: No cardiovascular contraindication.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: No cardiovascular contraindication.

learningObjective: Select anabolic therapy considering cardiovascular history.
author: AI draft

stem: A 69-year-old who has taken alendronate for 7 years has dull pain in her anterior thigh. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Reassure her that the pain is musculoskeletal and continue alendronate
Switch to zoledronic acid
Bilateral femur radiographs to evaluate for an atypical femoral fracture

rationale: Atypical femoral fractures are rare, rise with duration of therapy, and are often preceded by thigh or groin pain. Lesions may be bilateral.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Prodromal thigh pain on long-term bisphosphonate requires imaging.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Another bisphosphonate would add to the risk if a fracture is evolving.

learningObjective: Recognize prodromal symptoms of atypical femoral fracture.
author: AI draft

stem: Which statement about raloxifene is correct?

choices.text: It reduces hip fractures as much as bisphosphonates do
It is an effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms
It reduces vertebral fractures and ER-positive breast cancer

rationale: Raloxifene suits younger postmenopausal women at vertebral fracture risk who also have elevated breast cancer risk and no VTE history or bothersome VMS.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Hip fracture reduction has not been shown.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: It commonly worsens them.

learningObjective: Describe the benefit–risk profile of raloxifene.
author: AI draft

stem: After starting osteoporosis treatment, when is repeat DXA generally appropriate?

choices.text: Every 3 months, to titrate the dose
1 to 2 years after starting therapy
Never; DXA has no role during treatment

rationale: Follow-up should use the same machine where possible and focus on the spine and hip.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: BMD changes too slowly for this interval to be meaningful.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Follow-up DXA assesses response and guides holiday decisions.

author: AI draft

stem: A 62-year-old has newly diagnosed osteoporosis on DXA. What should be done before starting a bisphosphonate?

choices.text: Check calcium, vitamin D and renal function, and look for secondary causes
Start alendronate now; laboratory testing can wait until follow-up
Measure bone turnover markers only, and decide based on the result

rationale: Secondary causes such as hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption (eg, celiac disease), myeloma, hyperthyroidism and medications are common. Correcting vitamin D deficiency first lowers the risk of hypocalcemia.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Unrecognized hypocalcemia, vitamin D deficiency or renal disease can make treatment unsafe or ineffective.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Turnover markers do not replace evaluation for secondary causes.

author: AI draft

stem: A 29-year-old with POI takes transdermal estradiol and cyclic progesterone. She does not want to become pregnant. What is the best advice?

choices.text: Use contraception, because spontaneous pregnancy can occur
No contraception is needed, because POI means infertility
Her HT regimen also provides reliable contraception

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Roughly 5–10% of women with POI conceive spontaneously.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Physiologic HT doses do not reliably suppress ovulation.

author: AI draft

stem: How do estrogen doses for POI compare with those used for natural menopause?

choices.text: Lower doses, because young women have a higher VTE risk
Identical doses, stopped after 5 years of use
Higher doses, continued to about age 50–52

rationale: Estrogen replacement in POI aims to restore physiologic levels to protect bone, cardiovascular and cognitive health. Data from older women do not apply.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Young women with POI need doses that replace physiologic levels.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Treatment continues until around age 50–52.

learningObjective: Prescribe hormone replacement for POI.

stem: Which statement about systemic HT for breast cancer survivors is correct?

choices.text: It is safe once ER-positive disease has completed tamoxifen
It may be considered for refractory VMS, with oncology input
All estrogen, including vaginal products, is absolutely contraindicated

rationale: Nonhormone therapies are first-line for VMS in breast cancer survivors. For GSM, low-dose vaginal estrogen or DHEA may be considered after nonhormone options fail, with oncology input.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Hormone-receptor-positive disease remains a strong concern.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Low-dose vaginal estrogen or DHEA may be considered for GSM.

learningObjective: Apply HT guidance in breast cancer survivors.

stem: A 51-year-old whose mother had breast cancer at 68 has bothersome VMS. She has no other risk factors. What is the best counseling?

choices.text: HT is contraindicated by any first-degree family history
Family history alone is not a contraindication to HT
She must have genetic testing before HT can be considered

rationale: Observational evidence suggests HT does not further raise breast cancer risk in women at increased risk from a family history, or after BSO in BRCA carriers.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Observational data show HT does not further increase risk in women with a family history.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: A single relative diagnosed at 68 does not by itself meet criteria for testing.

learningObjective: Counsel about HT with a family history of breast cancer.

stem: A 56-year-old has endometrial hyperplasia without atypia on biopsy. She wants to avoid surgery. What is the preferred treatment?

choices.text: Levonorgestrel IUD
Hysterectomy is required
Observation while continuing unopposed estrogen

rationale: The LNG-IUD has higher regression rates, fewer adverse effects and a better bleeding profile than oral progestogens. Follow-up sampling is needed.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Hyperplasia without atypia is usually managed medically.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Unopposed estrogen must be stopped or opposed.

learningObjective: Manage endometrial hyperplasia without atypia.

stem: In which cancer survivor is hormone therapy generally NOT advised?

choices.text: A survivor of stage IA, grade 1 endometrioid endometrial cancer
A survivor of squamous cell cervical cancer
A survivor of uterine leiomyosarcoma or endometrial stromal sarcoma

rationale: HT is not advised after high-grade or advanced endometrial cancer or after endometrial stromal sarcoma or leiomyosarcoma, which may be hormone-sensitive.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: HT may be considered after early-stage, low-grade disease.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: Cervical squamous cancer is not hormone-dependent.

learningObjective: Identify cancer histories that contraindicate HT.

stem: In the WHI, what was the effect of estrogen plus progestin on colorectal cancer?

choices.text: Incidence and mortality both rose
Estrogen alone reduced risk more than estrogen plus progestin
Incidence was lower, but cancers were diagnosed at a more advanced stage

rationale: HT is not recommended for colorectal cancer prevention. Screening should begin at age 45 for average-risk women.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Incidence was reduced.
wrongAnswerRationales.b: The reduction was seen with EPT, not estrogen alone.

learningObjective: Recall WHI colorectal cancer findings.

stem: A 60-year-old has taken tamoxifen for 2 years and has no bleeding. She asks about endometrial cancer screening. What is recommended?

choices.text: Annual transvaginal ultrasound
Evaluate only if bleeding occurs
Annual endometrial biopsy

rationale: Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk in postmenopausal women, so any bleeding needs evaluation, but routine imaging of asymptomatic women is not recommended.

wrongAnswerRationales.a: Tamoxifen thickens the endometrium (subepithelial edema), so routine ultrasound causes false positives.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Routine sampling is not recommended without symptoms.

learningObjective: Apply endometrial surveillance guidance for tamoxifen users.

stem: A 44-year-old on tamoxifen for ER-positive breast cancer has had 12 months of amenorrhea after chemotherapy. Her oncologist is considering a switch to an aromatase inhibitor. What is the key concern?

choices.text: Ovarian function may recover, making an aromatase inhibitor alone ineffective
None, because 12 months of amenorrhea confirms menopause at any age
None, provided a single FSH level is above 40 IU/L

rationale: Aromatase inhibitors can stimulate ovarian function in premenopausal women. Serial estradiol testing, or ovarian suppression, is needed before relying on an AI.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Chemotherapy-induced amenorrhea is often reversible in women under 45.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: Single levels are unreliable, especially on tamoxifen.

learningObjective: Recognize the pitfalls of assuming menopause after chemotherapy.

stem: A 48-year-old had a hysterectomy with BSO for severe endometriosis and now starts estrogen therapy for VMS. Which consideration is most appropriate?

choices.text: Consider adding a progestogen to limit reactivation of residual disease
A progestogen is never indicated once the uterus has been removed
Estrogen is contraindicated after surgery for endometriosis

rationale: After surgical menopause for endometriosis, the benefits of estrogen generally outweigh the small risk of recurrence. Adding a progestogen may reduce the risk of reactivation or malignant transformation of residual implants.

wrongAnswerRationales.b: Residual endometriosis is an exception where some experts add a progestogen.
wrongAnswerRationales.c: HT is appropriate after surgical menopause; residual disease rarely recurs.

learningObjective: Tailor HT after hysterectomy for endometriosis.
